passage:
"Look at this!" Omkar held the phone out across the canteen table. "The constable told me to move my bike and I said, 'Do what you want.' Look at the views!"
Hemant watched the clip twice. Part of Hemant wanted those views too.
"You should try it next time we get stopped," Omkar said. "Just act bold."
"Weren't you scared? Your voice went up at the end."
"A bit."
"That's what I'm thinking about," Hemant said. "Staying calm would've taken more nerve. If it goes wrong, nobody in the comments walks into the station with you."
Omkar shrugged and pulled the phone back. "Maybe." But the phone stayed face down for the rest of lunch.

qa.q: What did Omkar say to the constable, according to the story?
What does Hemant feel while watching the clip, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hemant feels a pull to copy; the passage says part of Hemant wanted those views too, yet Hemant asks about the fear in Omkar's voice.

qa.q: What could Hemant say next time a friend pushes to film a stand-off?
qa.a: That staying calm and safe matters more than views, and that the comments will not help if things go wrong.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel about Hemant's comment?
qa.a: A little defensive but also thoughtful; admitting "A bit" and leaving the phone face down suggest the words landed.

grounding: A friend brags about talking back to police for a video; Hemant feels the pull to copy and chooses calm over likes.

passage:
Sunday. Lalit showed Suraj the clip on the school bus: Lalit on his scooter, arguing with a traffic constable, filming it himself. "You can't stop me, I know my rights!" Twelve thousand views. Suraj laughed with everyone, but his chest buzzed. He wanted that too, the likes, the looks in the corridor.

Wednesday. A checkpoint near the flyover. A constable waved Suraj's cousin's scooter over, and Suraj was riding pillion. His hand drifted to his phone. He could film. He could say something smart. Then he saw the constable's tired face and the queue of cars, and thought: this isn't a stage. He took his hand away and handed over the licence when asked. Two minutes, and they were waved on.

The next Monday. Lalit wasn't on the bus. His scooter had been seized after another argument, and his father had been called to the station. The clip was still up. Lalit wasn't laughing about it anymore.

qa.q: How many views did Lalit's clip get?
qa.a: Lalit's clip got twelve thousand views.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he watched the clip on the bus?
qa.a: Suraj felt a buzz of envy and excitement, wanting the same likes and attention Lalit was getting.

qa.q: Which choice at the checkpoint worked, and why?
qa.a: Putting the phone away and handing over the licence calmly worked, because it kept the stop short and safe instead of turning it into a show.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel about his clip after the scooter was seized?
qa.a: Lalit probably feels embarrassed and worried now, since the clip that brought likes also brought real trouble with his father and the police.

grounding: It shows a teen tempted to copy a friend who brags about talking back to police, who learns that staying calm is the braver choice and that a clip for likes can cost safety.

passage:
Ojas, I saw that video you were laughing at, the boy shouting at the policeman. Sit. Your Sarita Mausi has a story.

When I was sixteen, in Nagpur, my friend Rani was the bravest girl we knew. One evening a constable stopped a group of us near the lake for being out after dark. Rani put her hands on her hips and said, "Who are you to stop us? Do you know who my father is?" All of us giggled. I felt the pull to say something clever too, to be as bold as her.

I didn't. I don't know why. Maybe because my hands were shaking. I just said, "Sorry, sir, we are going home," and gave my name.

The constable let the rest of us go. Rani, he took to the chowki and called her father. She sat there till ten, crying.

Real courage that night was keeping quiet and getting everyone home. I learned that from my shaking hands.

qa.q: Where did the constable stop Sarita Mausi and her friends?
qa.a: He stopped them near the lake.

qa.q: What was young Sarita feeling when Rani talked back?
qa.a: Sarita felt a pull to be bold and clever like Rani, but also scared, with shaking hands.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sarita choosing to apologise and give her name instead of copying Rani was the turning point, because it got her home safely while Rani was taken to the chowki.

qa.q: What was it like for Rani at the chowki?
qa.a: Rani was probably frightened and ashamed, sitting there till ten and crying after her bold words backfired.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling a friend who talked back to police and the pull to copy her, and learning that courage can mean staying calm.
